- If sentiment is consistently negative (0.00–0.33) over recent days, reduce forecast slope and avoid upward momentum; model tends to overreact to negative sentiment.
- If sentiment spikes to 1.00 or 0.67 near the end of history, model often overestimates future prices — apply downward bias of 2–5% to forecast, especially if true outcome shows sharp drop.
- When model forecasts show steady upward trend (e.g., +0.01–0.03 per day) but true outcome shows mean reversion or sharp decline, reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days.
- If true outcome drops sharply after a forecast peak (e.g., 89.5 → 80.0), model often overshoots — apply “lag correction”: subtract 1–3% of forecast value for next 3–5 days.
- If sentiment history shows no clear trend (all 0.00) and forecast is flat, true outcome often exhibits volatility — increase forecast variance by ±1–2% to account for uncertainty.
- For 30-day forecasts, if last 3–5 days of history show strong downward trend, model often fails to recognize mean reversion — adjust forecast to target 1–2% below recent low if sentiment remains neutral or negative.
- If sentiment is positive but forecast is flat or rising slowly, true outcome often rises faster — increase forecast slope by 0.5–1.5% per day for next 3–5 days if sentiment remains positive.
